person.name: Erich_Kästner
person.summary: Erich Kästner was a German writer, poet, screenwriter, journalist, and satirist, best known for his socially critical verse and for modern, urban children’s books such as "Emil and the Detectives", "Pünktchen und Anton", "Das fliegende Klassenzimmer" and "Das doppelte Lottchen". Rising to prominence in Weimar Berlin, he chose to remain in Nazi Germany despite censorship and book burnings, wrote under pseudonyms, and survived wartime repression to become an influential post‑war public intellectual and children’s author based in Munich. In 1960 he received the international Hans Christian Andersen Award for his autobiography "Als ich ein kleiner Junge war".

chapters.headline: Dresden Childhood and War
chapters.description: Child of a lower‑middle‑class Dresden family, Kästner grew up as an only child, discovered books and writing early, and saw his schooling and youth shaped and scarred by the First World War.

chapters.headline: Studies and Leipzig Journalism
chapters.description: After the war Kästner completed his education, studied in Leipzig and other universities, and financed himself as a sharp‑tongued journalist and theatre critic, laying the foundations of his literary career.

chapters.headline: Weimar Berlin and Breakthrough
chapters.description: In late‑Weimar Berlin Kästner became a prolific publicist and poet, created his most famous children’s books and the novel "Fabian", and rose to fame as a leading voice of Neue Sachlichkeit.

chapters.headline: Under Nazism and War
chapters.description: Refusing to emigrate after 1933, Kästner endured bans and surveillance in Berlin, continued to write under pseudonyms including for film, and witnessed the destruction of his home during the Second World War.

chapters.headline: Post‑war Munich and Later Years
chapters.description: After 1945 Kästner resettled in Munich, re‑established himself as a writer of children’s books, essays and memoir, became a prominent moral commentator in the Federal Republic, and was honored internationally until his death.

events.title: Birth in Dresden
events.description: Erich Kästner is born in Dresden as the only child of saddler Emil Richard Kästner and his wife Ida, née Augustin. The family belongs to the lower middle class and lives in the [[Äußere Neustadt|Äußere Neustadt district]], a milieu that later provides detailed settings and social types for many of his books.

images.caption: Erich Kästner memorial at Albertplatz in Dresden, the city where he was born in 1899.

\u00c4u\u00dfere Neustadt.explanation: Äußere Neustadt is a densely built late-19th-century district of Dresden, historically a lower-middle-class and artisan neighborhood that shaped Erich Kästner’s social observations and later literary settings.

events.title: Enters teacher training institute
events.description: Following strong influence from the many schoolteachers who rented rooms in his parents’ flat, Kästner begins training as a primary‑school teacher at the [[Freiherrlich von Fletchersches Lehrerseminar|Freiherrlich von Fletchersches Lehrerseminar]] in Dresden‑Neustadt. He lives under strict, quasi‑military discipline he later dubs a "Lehrerkaserne", and starts publishing formally adept if conventional poems in the school paper, gaining his first experience as a writer.

images.caption: Erich Kästner memorial at Albertplatz in Dresden, near the district where he attended the Freiherrlich von Fletchersches Lehrerseminar.

Freiherrlich von Fletchersches Lehrersem.explanation: A privately endowed Saxon teacher‑training college in Dresden’s Neustadt district that prepared primary‑school teachers under a strict, quasi‑military regimen in the late 19th and early 20th centuries.

events.title: Frontline artillery training and injury
events.description: Drafted into military service during the First World War, Kästner joins a one‑year volunteer company of heavy artillery and is later sent to the [[Artillerie‑Mess‑Schule|Artillerie‑Mess‑Schule near Cologne‑Wahn]]. The brutal drill under an instructor named Sergeant Waurich leaves him with a lasting heart weakness and turns him into a convinced antimilitarist, an experience he processes in his bitter poem "Sergeant Waurich" and in lifelong hostility to militarism.

Artillerie\u2011Mess\u2011Schule.explanation: A specialized German Army artillery surveying and range‑finding school near Cologne‑Wahn in the First World War, where soldiers were trained in technical fire‑control and targeting methods.

events.title: Begins university studies in Leipzig
events.description: After the war Kästner completes his schooling with distinction, winning the Golden Scholarship of the city of Dresden, which binds him to study in Saxony. He enrolls at the University of Leipzig to study history, philosophy, German literature, newspaper science, and theatre studies, marking his transition from teacher‑training to an academic and literary path.

images.caption: Erich-Kästner-Schule, an elementary school in Leipzig-Gohlis, reflecting Erich Kästner's later commemoration in the city where he began his university studies in 1919.

events.title: Starts friendship with Erich Ohser
events.description: While studying and freelancing in Leipzig, Kästner meets the graphic artist Erich Ohser, later famous under the pseudonym "e. o. plauen" for his "Vater und Sohn" cartoons. Their friendship leads to joint projects combining Kästner’s texts and Ohser’s drawings, an early example of the close collaboration between text and illustration that will characterize Kästner’s children’s books.

images.caption: Portrait drawing of Erich Kästner by Erich Ohser from 1929, exemplifying their close writer–illustrator collaboration that began in the 1920s.

events.title: Earns doctorate in philosophy
events.description: Kästner submits his doctoral dissertation in German studies under Professor Georg Witkowski at the University of Leipzig and is awarded the degree of Dr. phil. Financing his studies increasingly through journalism and theatre criticism, he consolidates his dual identity as a scholar of literature and a working feuilletonist.

events.title: Moves to Berlin as freelance writer
events.description: After being dismissed from the Neue Leipziger Zeitung for an allegedly frivolous, mildly indecent poem illustrated by Erich Ohser, Kästner moves to Berlin, then the cultural capital of the Weimar Republic. Writing under pseudonyms such as "Berthold Bürger", he works as a free‑lance cultural correspondent and begins to place poems, glosses, and essays in leading newspapers and magazines, laying the groundwork for his reputation as a sharp social satirist.

images.caption: Dust jacket illustrated by Erich Ohser for Erich Kästner’s poetry volume "Gesang zwischen den Stühlen" (1932), reflecting the kind of satirical literary work he was developing after his move to Berlin.

events.title: Publishes first poetry collection
events.description: Kästner brings out his first book, "Herz auf Taille", a collection of socially observant, witty poems, many written during his Leipzig years. The volume, with its blend of irony, sentiment, and clear language, makes him a recognized voice of the [[Neue Sachlichkeit|Neue Sachlichkeit movement]] and broadens his readership beyond newspaper audiences.

images.caption: Title page of Erich Kästner's early 1930s book "Emil und die Detektive", representative of the era in which his first poetry collection "Herz auf Taille" was published.

Neue Sachlichkeit.explanation: A German cultural movement of the 1920s that rejected Expressionism in favor of a sober, realistic, and socially critical style in literature, art, and architecture.

events.title: Breakthrough with "Emil und die Detektive"
events.description: At the urging of Berlin children’s publisher Edith Jacobsohn, Kästner publishes his first children’s novel, "Emil und die Detektive", set in contemporary Berlin and illustrated by Walter Trier. The fast‑paced urban adventure becomes an unprecedented success, selling over two million copies in Germany alone and being translated into dozens of languages, and it establishes him internationally as an innovator of modern children’s literature.

images.caption: Signature of German writer Erich Kästner, whose 1929 children’s novel "Emil und die Detektive" became a landmark of modern children’s literature.

events.title: Releases novel "Fabian"
events.description: Kästner publishes the novel "Fabian – Die Geschichte eines Moralisten", a montage‑like, cinematic portrait of late‑Weimar Berlin seen through the eyes of an unemployed Germanist. With its sharp critique of the moral and political decay of the republic and its mix of irony and despair, the book strengthens his position as a major contemporary novelist as well as a children’s author.

images.caption: German author Erich Kästner around 1930, shortly before the publication of his novel "Fabian – Die Geschichte eines Moralisten" in 1931.

events.title: Decides to remain in Nazi Germany
events.description: After [[Hitler’s appointment as Reich Chancellor|Hitler’s appointment as Reich Chancellor]], many regime‑critical writers emigrate, but Kästner consciously chooses to stay in Germany, initially believing the dictatorship will be short‑lived. Although fully aware that his antimilitarist and satirical texts make him a target, he opts to witness events from within, a decision that shapes his life for the next twelve years.

images.caption: Portrait photograph of Erich Kästner taken in Berlin between 1930 and 1945, around the period when he decided to remain in Nazi Germany.

Hitler\u2019s appointment as Reich Chanc.explanation: On 30 January 1933, President Paul von Hindenburg appointed Adolf Hitler to the office of Reich Chancellor of Germany, marking the beginning of the Nazi dictatorship.

events.title: Books burned and banned by Nazis
events.description: On the night of the [[Nazi book burnings|Nazi book burnings]], copies of Kästner’s works are consigned to the flames on German university squares alongside those of many other "un‑German" authors. His books are soon placed on blacklists and prohibited throughout the Reich. Kästner, who witnesses the burning in Berlin, becomes one of the few major authors whose existing oeuvre is totally banned while he himself remains in the country under surveillance.

images.caption: Erich Kästner memorial at Albertplatz in Dresden, commemorating the German author whose works were banned and burned by the Nazis in 1933.

Nazi book burnings.explanation: A coordinated campaign on 10 May 1933 in which Nazi student groups, with official backing, publicly burned books across Germany that were deemed "un‑German", targeting works by Jewish, socialist, pacifist, and other politically or culturally suspect authors.

events.title: Writes film script for "Münchhausen" under pseudonym
events.description: Despite bans on his name, Kästner manages to work in the [[UFA|Nazi-era German film industry]] by using pseudonyms, notably contributing to the screenplay of the lavish color film "Münchhausen" for UFA in 1943. This anonymous screenwriting provides him with income and a covert way to continue literary activity under dictatorship, even as he remains under Gestapo suspicion.

UFA.explanation: Universum Film AG was the dominant state-controlled film studio in Nazi Germany, producing major propaganda and entertainment films.

events.title: Berlin apartment destroyed in air raid
events.description: During a heavy Allied air raid on Berlin, Kästner’s flat in the Roscherstraße burns out completely, destroying a large part of his manuscripts, correspondence, and clippings from his extraordinarily prolific journalistic output between 1923 and 1933. The loss contributes to the fragmentary survival of much of his early journalism and personal archive.

events.title: Relocates to Munich after the war
events.description: With the collapse of the Nazi regime and Germany’s defeat, Kästner moves from devastated Berlin to Munich, in the American zone of occupation. There he resumes publishing under his own name, writes for newspapers and radio, and begins to reissue and continue his children’s books and essays, quickly becoming an important cultural voice in the early Federal Republic.

images.caption: Citation plaque for Erich Kästner near Irschenhausen in Bavaria, commemorating his connection with the Munich region where he settled after the war.

events.title: Publishes "Das doppelte Lottchen"
events.description: Kästner publishes the children’s novel "Das doppelte Lottchen", about separated twin girls who meet at a holiday camp and scheme to reunite their divorced parents. Written in the shadow of war’s dislocations yet maintaining his light, humorous tone, the book becomes one of his most beloved works and is adapted into numerous films, including Disney’s "The Parent Trap".

images.caption: Villa Augustin in Dresden, now the Erich Kästner Museum dedicated to the author's life and works, including his children's books such as "Das doppelte Lottchen".

events.title: Receives Hans Christian Andersen Award
events.description: In recognition of his lasting contribution to children’s literature, particularly his autobiographical work "Als ich ein kleiner Junge war" and his innovative novels for young readers, Kästner is awarded the international Hans Christian Andersen Medal. The prize cements his reputation worldwide as one of the 20th century’s most important children’s authors.

images.caption: Memorial dedicated to Erich Kästner in Dresden, Germany, commemorating his legacy as a major 20th‑century children's author.

events.title: Death in Munich
events.description: Erich Kästner dies in Munich at the age of seventy‑five after a long illness. By the time of his death he is revered both as the witty chronicler of Weimar and post‑war society and as the creator of enduring children’s classics that continue to be read and adapted worldwide.

images.caption: Erich Kästner in Munich in 1968 during filming for a North German Broadcasting (NDR) television feature, a few years before his death in the city.
